en: Mayon Volcano in Albay is famous for its perfectly symmetrical cone shape that is clearly visible from surrounding towns.
Hikers climbing Mount Pulag in Benguet often observe a thick sea of clouds forming just above the mountain tree line.
The Cagayan River flows northward through the Cagayan Valley, making it the longest river in the Philippines.
Laguna de Bay is so large that people on its shores can see the sun setting directly over its vast freshwater surface.
The rare waling-waling orchid is an epiphyte, meaning you can observe it growing high on the branches of tall rainforest trees.
During the amihan season from November to February, you can feel cool, dry northeast winds blowing across most of the Philippines.
Inside the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River, visitors can observe massive stalactites and stalagmites formed over thousands of years by dripping mineral water.
Snorkelers at Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park can observe vibrant coral formations teeming with diverse marine life in exceptionally clear ocean waters.
The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes that are each larger than its brain, helping it see clearly to hunt insects at night.
The Banaue Rice Terraces show how farmers carved step-like fields into steep mountains to grow rice and prevent heavy rains from washing away soil.
Taal Volcano is unique because you can observe a smaller volcanic island sitting directly inside the large freshwater expanse of Taal Lake.
Inside the limestone caves of Palawan, you can observe millions of wrinkled bats flying out at dusk to hunt for insects.
